title: Variables & Data Types
overview: Every program works with data. In this lecture you'll learn how to store data using variables, and understand the different kinds of data Python can handle — numbers, text, and more.

blocks.content: Imagine you write your friend's phone number on a sticky note and stick it to your desk. Whenever you need to call them, you don't try to memorize it again — you just look at the sticky note.
**Variables work exactly like that sticky note.** They give a name to a piece of information so you can use it later without having to repeat yourself.
In Python, you create a variable using the `=` sign. The name goes on the left, the value goes on the right.

blocks.title: Try It — Creating Variables
blocks.code:
name = "Lakshanya"
age = 20
city = "Chennai"

print(name)
print(age)
print(city)

blocks.content: Notice that we only wrote `"Lakshanya"` once, but we can use the variable `name` as many times as we want. That's the whole point — store once, use anywhere.
Variables can also be updated. The new value simply replaces the old one.

blocks.title: Try It — Updating a Variable
blocks.code:
score = 0
print(score)

score = 10
print(score)

score = score + 5
print(score)

analogy.title: Labeled Sticky Note
analogy.description: A sticky note has a label (the variable name) and a value written on it. You can update the note any time by erasing and rewriting.
bullets: It has a label on the front that tells you what it contains.
The note itself stores information you want to keep.
You can peel it off and rewrite the content any time you want.
analogy.highlightCard: A sticky note has a label and stores a value — exactly like a Python variable.

visualization.title: Variable = Label + Value
bullets: A variable has a name, just like the label on the sticky note.
It stores a value, just like the information written on the note.
You can read or update the variable at any point in your program.
visualization.highlightCard: variable = name + value. That's the entire idea.

highlights: name = assigns a value to the variable on the left.
Use the variable name to access its stored value later.
Python remembers the value for the entire program after assignment.
code.highlightCard: Variables let Python store and remember information throughout your program.

reflection.question: What does a variable store?
reflection.answer: A variable stores a named value that can be used and updated throughout your program.
options: A named value of any type

blocks.stage1Transition: So how does Python remember information? Let's translate this into code.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how variables look in actual Python code.
blocks.takeaway: A variable is like a labeled sticky note in Python's memory — it has a name and stores a value you can read and change at any time.

blocks.title: Store a Student Profile
blocks.instructions: Your college management system needs to store basic student info. Create three variables — student_name, roll_number, and department — then print each one.
blocks.starterCode:
# Store student information
student_name = ""
roll_number = ""
department = ""

# Print each variable
blocks.solution:
student_name = "Priya"
roll_number = "RA2011004"
department = "Computer Science"

print(student_name)
print(roll_number)
print(department)
blocks.hint: Text values need quotes. Numbers don't require quotes but you can use them as strings here since roll numbers often have letters.

blocks.content: Variable names can be almost anything — but Python has a few rules you must follow.

**Rule 1:** Start with a letter or underscore (`_`), never a number.

**Rule 2:** Use only letters, numbers, and underscores.

**Rule 3:** Python is case-sensitive. `name` and `Name` are two completely different variables.

**Rule 4:** Never use Python's reserved keywords as variable names (like `if`, `for`, `print`, `while`).

blocks.title: Try It — Valid vs Invalid Names
blocks.code:
# Valid names
student_name = "Ravi"
age2 = 21
_score = 95

# These would cause errors:
# 2name = "Ravi"   ← starts with number
# my-score = 95   ← hyphen not allowed

print(student_name, age2, _score)

blocks.content: A convention (not a rule) is to use **snake_case** — lowercase words separated by underscores. Python developers worldwide use this style.

Good names: `student_name`, `total_marks`, `phone_number`

Bad names: `x`, `a1`, `data2` — these tell you nothing about what's stored inside.

analogy.title: Folder Label in an Office
analogy.description: In a filing cabinet, folders have clear labels: 'Tax Documents 2024', 'Medical Records'. A vague label like 'Stuff' wastes everyone's time. Variable names work the same way.
bullets: Clear labels let you find the right folder immediately.
A label like 'Stuff' is useless — you have no idea what's inside.
Good labels tell you exactly what a folder contains at a glance.
analogy.highlightCard: Good variable names make your code self-explanatory to anyone who reads it.

visualization.title: Is this a good variable name?
visualization.condition: Is the name descriptive and follows rules?
bullets: Descriptive names like student_score are immediately clear.
Vague names like x or a tell nobody anything about the value.
Python uses underscores to separate words in variable names.
visualization.highlightCard: Name variables so clearly that a stranger instantly understands what they store.

highlights: x = 89 is valid Python but tells nobody what 89 means.
student_score = 89 makes the purpose obvious to any reader.
Python convention: use lowercase_with_underscores for variable names.
code.highlightCard: Always choose variable names that clearly describe what they store.

reflection.question: Which is the best variable name for storing a phone number?
reflection.answer: phone_number — it's descriptive, follows Python naming conventions, and is immediately clear.

blocks.stage1Transition: How do we name our variables well in Python? Let's see what good naming looks like.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is the difference between good and bad variable names in Python.
blocks.takeaway: Just like filing cabinet folders need clear labels, your variable names should instantly communicate what they store. Clear names make programs easy to read and maintain.

blocks.title: Fix the Variable Names
blocks.instructions: A junior developer wrote the code below with poor variable names. Rewrite it using proper snake_case names that actually describe what's stored. The output should stay the same.
blocks.starterCode:
# Rename these variables properly
x = "Mumbai"
a = 28
b = 92.5

print(x)
print(a)
print(b)
blocks.solution:
city_name = "Mumbai"
student_age = 28
average_score = 92.5

print(city_name)
print(student_age)
print(average_score)
blocks.hint: x is a city name, a is someone's age, b is an average score. Use snake_case.

blocks.content: Not all data is the same. A person's name is different from their age, which is different from their bank balance, which is different from whether they passed an exam.
Python has different **data types** to handle different kinds of information. The four you'll use most often:

**int** — whole numbers. `age = 20`, `students = 45`

**float** — decimal numbers. `gpa = 8.75`, `price = 299.99`

**str** — text (string). `name = "Priya"`, `city = "Delhi"`

**bool** — True or False. `is_enrolled = True`, `has_id = False`

blocks.title: Try It — All Four Types
blocks.code:
name = "Arjun"          # str
age = 19               # int
gpa = 9.2              # float
is_enrolled = True     # bool

print(type(name))
print(type(age))
print(type(gpa))
print(type(is_enrolled))

blocks.content: `type()` is a built-in function that tells you what type of data a variable holds. It's extremely useful when debugging.
Python is **dynamically typed** — you don't need to declare the type. Python figures it out from what you assign. `age = 20` makes it an int automatically.

analogy.title: Different Containers for Different Items
analogy.description: In a kitchen: eggs go in egg cartons, milk goes in bottles, spices go in small jars. Each container matches the type of content. Python data types work the same way.
bullets: Eggs go in egg cartons — not milk bottles or spice jars.
Each container is specifically designed for its content type.
Forcing the wrong content into the wrong container causes problems.
analogy.highlightCard: Python has different data types — each one holds a different kind of value.

visualization.title: Data Type Containers
bullets: str holds text wrapped in quotes — like 'Hello' or 'Rohan'.
int holds whole numbers like 42 or 100.
float holds decimal numbers like 3.14 or 8.75.
bool holds only True or False — nothing else.
visualization.highlightCard: Use the right type for the right value — int, float, str, or bool.

code.code:
marks = 87      # int
percentage = 87.5  # float
grade = "A"    # str
passed = True  # bool
print(marks, percentage, grade, passed)
highlights: 87 without quotes is an int — Python stores it as a whole number.
87.5 is a float — the decimal point makes it different from int.
"A" in quotes is a str — Python treats it as text, not a number.
code.highlightCard: Python automatically detects the type from the value you assign.

reflection.question: What type would you use to store a student's CGPA like 8.75?
reflection.answer: float — because 8.75 has a decimal point. int would truncate it to 8.

blocks.stage1Transition: How does Python know what type of value is stored? That's where data types come in.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how different data types look in real Python code.
blocks.takeaway: Python data types are like containers — int for whole numbers, float for decimals, str for text, bool for True/False. Always put your data in the right container.

keyTakeaways.text: A variable is a named container that stores a value you can use later.
Create a variable with the = sign: name = "value".
Variable names must start with a letter or underscore, not a number.
Python is case-sensitive: name and Name are different variables.
Use snake_case for readability: student_name, not studentname.
int stores whole numbers, float stores decimals, str stores text, bool stores True/False.
Python automatically figures out the data type — you don't need to declare it.
Use type() to check the data type of any variable.

whatYouLearned: What a variable is and how to create one
How to update a variable's value
Python naming rules and snake_case convention
The four main data types: int, float, str, bool

quiz.question: Which of the following is a valid Python variable name?
quiz.explanation: Variable names cannot start with a number (2score), cannot contain hyphens (my-score), and cannot contain spaces (my score). Only my_score follows all Python naming rules.

quiz.question:
What will this code print?
x = 5
x = x + 3
print(x)
quiz.explanation: x starts as 5. Then x = x + 3 means x = 5 + 3 = 8. The variable is updated, and print(x) outputs the new value 8.

quiz.question: What data type is the value 3.14?
quiz.explanation: Any number with a decimal point is a float in Python. Whole numbers (no decimal) are int. 3.14 has a decimal point, so it's a float.

quiz.question: What will type("Hello") return?
quiz.explanation: Python's type() function returns the full class name. For text values, it returns <class 'str'>. The quotes make "Hello" a string (str).

quiz.question: Which value is a boolean?
quiz.explanation: Python booleans are the keywords True and False (capital first letter, no quotes). "True" in quotes is a string, 1 is an integer, and yes is neither a Python keyword nor a boolean.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of using descriptive variable names like student_name instead of x?
options: It makes code easier to read and understand
quiz.answer: It makes code easier to read and understand
quiz.explanation: Descriptive names are a convention that makes your code self-documenting. When you or someone else reads the code later, student_name immediately tells you what's stored. x tells you nothing.

problems.title: Shop Item Card
problems.description:
Create variables to represent a product in a shop:
- product_name (str): any product you like
- price (float): its price with decimal
- quantity (int): how many in stock
- is_available (bool): True if in stock

Print all four variables.
problems.solution:
product_name = "Wireless Mouse"
price = 799.99
quantity = 50
is_available = True

print(product_name)
print(price)
print(quantity)
print(is_available)

problems.title: Temperature Converter Variables
problems.description:
Store two temperatures:
- temp_celsius as 37.5 (float)
- temp_unit as "Celsius" (str)

Then update temp_celsius to 100.0 and print both variables again.

Expected output:
37.5
Celsius
100.0
Celsius
problems.solution:
temp_celsius = 37.5
temp_unit = "Celsius"

print(temp_celsius)
print(temp_unit)

temp_celsius = 100.0
print(temp_celsius)
print(temp_unit)

problems.title: Swap Two Variables
problems.description:
Create two variables:
- a = "Hello"
- b = "World"

Swap their values so that a becomes "World" and b becomes "Hello".
Print a and b after the swap.

Expected output:
World
Hello
problems.starterCode:
a = "Hello"
b = "World"

# Swap the values of a and b
# (Hint: you might need a temporary variable)
problems.solution:
a = "Hello"
b = "World"

temp = a
a = b
b = temp

print(a)
print(b)

testCases.label: a is World, b is Hello
